passages.title: Listen before joining others
passages.summary: The book opens by stating its purpose: to teach wisdom, justice, and good sense. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. A parent tells a son to listen to his father and mother. Sinners will invite him to ambush the innocent and share the loot. He must not go with them. They set a trap for their own lives. Then Wisdom calls aloud in the street like a woman. Those who refuse her will eat the fruit of their own choices.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me explains fearing God as love and obedience. Why does Wisdom warn that the violent men trap themselves?

contextNote.title: Wisdom begins with relationships
contextNote.text: Verse 8 names two teachers, a father and a mother. The mother’s teaching stands beside the father’s instruction. Verse 9 calls their words a wreath and a necklace. The first lesson that follows is about an invitation (verses 10–14). A gang says, “Come with us,” and promises one shared purse. The learner must choose between two sets of voices. Verses 18–19 say the violent men ambush themselves.

passages.title: Search for wisdom
passages.summary: The teacher tells his son to accept his words and store up his commands. He must turn his ear to wisdom and call out for understanding. He must seek it like silver and search for it like hidden treasure. Then he will understand the fear of the LORD. The LORD gives wisdom and guards the path of the just. Good sense will protect the learner from men who speak twisted things. It will protect him from the unfaithful wife. The upright will remain in the land.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me invites readers to seek wisdom from God. Which actions does the teacher compare with searching for treasure?

contextNote.title: Learning requires a search
contextNote.text: Verses 1–4 stack up conditions with the word “if.” Verse 5 answers with “then.” Verse 4 compares the search to mining for silver. Miners dig long and deep for what they value. Yet verse 6 says the LORD gives wisdom. The chapter holds both together. A person must search hard, and what he finds is still a gift.

passages.title: Trust God and help neighbors
passages.summary: The teacher tells his son to keep kindness and truth close. He should trust the LORD with all his heart, not his own insight. He should honor the LORD with his wealth. The LORD corrects those he loves, as a father does. Wisdom is worth more than silver and is a tree of life. The learner must not hold back good from one who is owed it. He must not tell a neighbor to come back tomorrow. He must not plot against a neighbor who lives trustingly beside him.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me teaches trust in the Lord. Why should the learner help a neighbor today rather than tomorrow?

contextNote.title: Trust reaches a neighbor’s need
contextNote.text: The chapter begins with trust in God (verses 5–6). It ends with neighbors (verses 27–30). Verse 27 speaks of good that is “due” to someone. The neighbor has a claim, and the learner has the means. Verse 28 names a common way to refuse: come again tomorrow. Delay can be a quiet form of saying no. Trust in God shows itself in prompt help.

passages.title: Choose a path carefully
passages.summary: A father tells his sons to listen and gain understanding. He says he was once a tender son himself. His own father taught him to get wisdom above all else. He warns against the path of the wicked. The path of the righteous is like dawn that grows to full day. The learner must guard his heart, for life flows from it. He must keep his mouth honest and his eyes straight ahead. He must make his path level and not turn aside.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the path image with following the Lord. How do speech, sight, and steps affect the path the learner follows?

contextNote.title: A father repeats what he received
contextNote.text: In verse 3 the teacher remembers being a child. His father taught him the words he now repeats (verse 4). Three generations stand in these verses. The teaching is handed on; the father did not invent it. Verse 23 puts the heart first as the source of life. Verses 24–27 then name the mouth, the eyes, and the feet. Guarding the inside comes before guarding the steps.

passages.title: Remain faithful to your wife
passages.summary: The teacher warns his son about another man’s wife. Her lips drip honey, but the end is bitter. Her steps lead down to death. He must stay far from her door. Otherwise strangers will take his strength and wealth, and he will groan at the end. He should drink water from his own well. He should rejoice in the wife of his youth. A man’s ways are before the LORD, and his own sins bind him.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What costs does the teacher describe beyond the first attraction?

contextNote.title: Water images distinguish shared commitment from wandering
contextNote.text: Verses 15–18 speak of faithfulness through pictures of water. A cistern, a well, springs, and a fountain are named. In a dry land a household’s water was precious and guarded. Verse 16 pictures it spilled in the streets and wasted. The chapter does more than forbid. Verses 18–19 tell the man to delight in his own wife. The warning rests on a good thing worth keeping.

passages.title: Promises, work, and harmful acts
passages.summary: The teacher warns against pledging to cover another person’s debt. If the son has done so, he must free himself at once. He tells the lazy person to watch the ant. She has no ruler and still stores food in summer. A little extra sleep brings poverty like a robber. A troublemaker winks and stirs up quarrels. The LORD hates seven things, including lying and shedding innocent blood. Adultery is like carrying fire in one’s lap.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does the ant’s work differ from the sleeper’s choices?

contextNote.title: Different dangers share a need for attention
contextNote.text: Verse 6 sends the learner to watch an insect. Wisdom can be gained by looking closely at the created world. Verse 7 notes that the ant has no chief or overseer. She works without being told. Verse 8 adds that she works at the right season. The chapter covers debts, laziness, troublemakers, and adultery. In each case a small lapse of attention leads to a large loss.

passages.title: A learner follows a tempting invitation
passages.summary: The teacher tells his son to treat wisdom as a sister. Then he describes what he saw from his window. A young man without sense walked near a certain woman’s corner at dusk. She came out dressed to attract him and seized and kissed him. She said she had made offerings and prepared her bed with fine linen. Her husband was away on a long journey. He followed her like an ox going to slaughter. Her house is the road to the grave.
passages.uncertainty: Egypt names the cloth’s origin, not the scene’s location.

lds.text: Which details show the difference between her promises and the danger?

contextNote.title: A warning unfolds as a scene
contextNote.text: The warning comes as a scene the teacher watched (verses 6–7). The details matter. Verse 8 says the youth walked toward her corner, so he chose the street. Verse 9 marks the time as twilight turning to dark. Her speech uses religion (verse 14) and promises no one will know (verses 19–20). Verses 22–23 compare him to an ox, a deer, and a bird. A story lets the learner see the steps before the fall.

passages.title: Wisdom speaks in public
passages.summary: Wisdom calls out on the heights and at the city gates. She speaks to all people and says her words are true. She is better than silver, gold, and rubies. By her kings rule justly. She loves those who love her. The LORD had her at the beginning, before the mountains and the seas. She was beside him when he marked out the earth’s foundations. Whoever finds her finds life.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me points to the rejection of evil in verse 13. How does Wisdom’s public invitation differ from the woman’s invitation in chapter 7?

contextNote.title: Wisdom speaks beyond the household
contextNote.text: Wisdom speaks in the open, at the gates where everyone passes (verse 3). The woman of chapter 7 worked at dusk in a side street. In verse 22 Wisdom gives her age. She was with the LORD before any of his works. Verses 27–30 place her beside him at creation. So living wisely fits the way the world was made. Verses 30–31 add that she rejoiced in the world and in people.

passages.title: Two women invite the learner
passages.summary: Wisdom has built her house with seven pillars. She has prepared meat and wine and set her table. She sends her maids to call from the high places. She invites the simple to come in and eat. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. Folly is a loud woman who sits at her door. She calls to the simple with the same words. She offers stolen water, and her guests are in the grave.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What does Folly hide that Wisdom openly explains?

contextNote.title: Similar invitations conceal different endings
contextNote.text: Verse 4 and verse 16 are the same invitation, word for word. Two hosts call the same people in the same way. The learner must look past the words to what each has ready. Wisdom built a house and cooked a meal (verses 1–2). Folly offers stolen water and secret bread (verse 17). Verse 6 ends in life, and verse 18 ends among the dead. This chapter closes the book’s long opening lessons.

passages.title: Words and work affect others
passages.summary: Here the short sayings of Solomon begin. A wise son makes his father glad. Wealth gained by wrong does no good. Lazy hands make a person poor, and hard work brings wealth. Love covers all wrongs. Where words are many, sin is not far away. The lips of the righteous feed many people. When the storm passes, the wicked are gone, and the righteous stand.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does hatred stir up quarrels while love covers offenses?

contextNote.title: Short sayings require a supplied situation
contextNote.text: From this chapter the sayings stand alone, two lines each. The second line often contrasts with the first. No story surrounds them. The reader must supply the situation where each one fits. Verse 19 says more talk gives more room for wrong. Restraint of the lips is called wisdom. Many sayings in this chapter concern speech (verses 11, 13, 18, 20–21, 31–32).

passages.title: Honesty in trade and community
passages.summary: A false scale is hateful to the LORD, and honest weights please him. Pride brings shame, and humility brings wisdom. A city rejoices when the righteous do well. A gossip reveals secrets, and a trustworthy person keeps them. Many advisers bring safety. One person gives freely and gains more. Another holds back and becomes poor. People curse the one who hoards grain.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does withholding grain affect the people who need it?

contextNote.title: A proverb makes trade a moral decision
contextNote.text: Verse 1 calls a rigged scale an “abomination.” Other texts use that strong word for idols. Leviticus 19:35–36 and Deuteronomy 25:13–16 give the law behind it. A buyer could not easily test a seller’s weights. The poor, who bought in small amounts, were hurt most. An ancient trade weight shows the kind of tool the saying has in view. Verse 26 applies the same concern to those who hoard grain.

passages.title: Correction, work, and careful speech
passages.summary: Whoever loves correction loves knowledge. A worthy wife is her husband’s crown. A righteous person cares for the life of his animal. The one who works his land has bread. A fool thinks his own way is right. Rash words cut like a sword, and a wise tongue heals. Truthful lips last forever. Worry weighs a heart down, and a kind word makes it glad.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the chapter compare rash speech with a sword?

contextNote.title: Words can wound or heal
contextNote.text: Verse 18 treats words as a weapon or a medicine. The harmful speaker is called rash. He may not mean harm; he simply does not think first. The wound is as real as a sword cut. The wise tongue is said to heal. Verse 25 gives an example: one good word lifts a heavy heart. Verse 19 adds that true words last and lies do not.

passages.title: Choose teachers and companions
passages.summary: A wise son accepts his father’s teaching. The one who guards his mouth guards his life. Some pretend to be rich and have nothing. Wealth gained in haste shrinks away. Hope put off makes the heart sick. Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise. A poor person’s field may yield much food, and injustice sweeps it away. A parent who loves a child corrects him.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Scripture Helps applies the rod image to loving, consistent teaching. How does verse 23 challenge blaming every poor person for poverty?

contextNote.title: Delay gives desire a bodily cost
contextNote.text: Verse 12 gives no command. It describes what waiting does to a person. A hope delayed again and again makes the heart sick. A longing fulfilled is called a tree of life. Verse 19 repeats that a desire met is sweet. The saying helps a reader understand another person’s weariness. Verse 23 adds that poverty can come from injustice, not from laziness.

passages.title: Look beyond first impressions
passages.summary: A wise woman builds her house, and a foolish one tears it down. A way may seem right to a person and end in death. Even in laughter the heart may ache. The simple believe everything, and the careful watch their steps. The poor are shunned even by neighbors, and the rich have many friends. Whoever oppresses the poor insults their Maker. A calm heart gives life to the body. Righteousness lifts up a nation.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why should the learner look beyond laughter when judging someone’s happiness?

contextNote.title: Appearance can conceal grief
contextNote.text: This chapter keeps setting how things seem against how they are. Verse 12 says a road can look right and lead to death. Verse 13 applies that to a face. A person may laugh while the heart is in pain. Verse 10 says each heart knows its own bitterness. So the reader should be slow to judge by appearances. Verse 31 ties the treatment of the poor to respect for God.

passages.title: Answer gently and accept advice
passages.summary: A gentle answer turns away anger, and a harsh word stirs it up. The eyes of the LORD are in every place. A little with the fear of the LORD is better than great treasure with trouble. A meal of vegetables with love is better than rich meat with hatred. Plans fail without advice. A word spoken at the right time is good. The LORD hears the prayer of the righteous. Humility comes before honor.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me teaches kind words and patient answers. How do gentle words change the direction of a quarrel?

contextNote.title: Speech changes the direction of conflict
contextNote.text: Verse 1 says the direction of a quarrel depends on the reply. A gentle answer is not a weak one. It “turns away” wrath, which is an active result. A harsh word feeds the fire. Verse 18 says a patient person calms a dispute. Verse 28 says the righteous think before they answer. Verse 23 praises the word that comes at the right moment.

passages.title: Plans need humility and self-control
passages.summary: People make plans in their hearts, and the answer comes from the LORD. A person’s ways seem pure to him, and the LORD weighs motives. Honest scales belong to the LORD. Pride goes before destruction. Pleasant words are like honey. Gray hair is a crown of glory. One who controls his temper is better than one who captures a city. The lot is cast, and its every decision is from the LORD.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me applies these sayings to how people communicate. Why does the chapter value controlling anger above capturing a city?

contextNote.title: Planning does not give complete control
contextNote.text: Verse 9 keeps two truths together. People plan their course, and the saying does not discourage that. The LORD directs the actual steps. Verses 1 and 33 make the same point at the chapter’s two ends. Outcomes are not fully in human hands. That leads to the warning about pride in verse 18. Verse 32 values rule over oneself above victory in war.

passages.title: Peace, friendship, and fair judgment
passages.summary: A dry crust with peace is better than a house full of feasting with strife. The LORD tests hearts as fire tests silver and gold. Whoever mocks the poor insults their Maker. One who covers an offense seeks love. A friend loves at all times. To clear the guilty and condemn the innocent are both hateful to the LORD. A cheerful heart is good medicine. Even a fool seems wise when he keeps silent.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How do repeated accusations damage a friendship?

contextNote.title: Peace changes the value of abundance
contextNote.text: Verse 1 is a “better than” saying. It compares a dry scrap with a table full of meat. The peace at the table decides which is better. A feast with quarreling is the poorer meal. Sayings in 15:16–17 make the same judgment. Verse 14 adds advice on how to keep that peace. A quarrel starts like a leak in a dam, so stop it early.

passages.title: Listen before answering
passages.summary: A person who keeps apart seeks only his own desire. A fool takes no pleasure in understanding and only airs his opinions. The name of the LORD is a strong tower. A rich man imagines his wealth is a high wall. To answer before listening is folly and shame. The first to state a case seems right until the other side questions him. Death and life are in the power of the tongue. Some friends stay closer than a brother.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why should a judge hear more than the first person’s account?

contextNote.title: A hearing must precede judgment
contextNote.text: Verse 13 states a basic rule of fairness and of courtesy. A person must hear before he answers. Verse 17 applies the rule to disputes. The first speaker sounds right until the other side is heard. Verse 2 describes the opposite habit. The fool wants to talk and not to understand. Verse 15 says the ear of the wise seeks knowledge.

passages.title: Wealth changes how people treat neighbors
passages.summary: It is better to be poor and honest than a liar and a fool. Zeal without knowledge is not good. Wealth brings many friends, and a poor person loses the one he has. A false witness will not go unpunished. Good sense makes a person slow to anger. Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD. People make many plans, and the LORD’s purpose stands. A lazy person will not even lift his hand to his mouth.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does the chapter expose friendships that depend on wealth?

contextNote.title: Wealth can distort friendship
contextNote.text: Verse 4 reports a fact about money and friendship. It does not approve of it. Verses 6–7 add that even a poor man’s brothers avoid him. The chapter then judges what it has observed. Verse 17 says kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD. Verses 1 and 22 say an honest poor person is better than a liar. The saying trains the reader to notice how wealth bends loyalty.

passages.title: Trade honestly and avoid revenge
passages.summary: Wine is a mocker, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise. It is an honor to stay out of a quarrel. A person’s purpose is like deep water, and a wise one draws it out. No one can say his heart is fully clean. The LORD hates unequal weights and measures. A buyer says “It’s no good” and then boasts of his bargain. Do not say you will repay evil. Wait for the LORD.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What does the buyer’s changed story reveal about his honesty?

contextNote.title: Fair judgment begins in ordinary tools
contextNote.text: Verse 10 speaks of “differing weights.” A cheating trader kept two sets, one heavy and one light. He bought with one and sold with the other. Deuteronomy 25:13–14 forbids keeping both in the bag. Verse 23 repeats the saying in this same chapter. Verse 14 shows the buyer lying too. An ancient trade weight shows the kind of tool the saying has in view.

passages.title: Justice matters more than offerings
passages.summary: A king’s heart is in the LORD’s hand like a stream of water. The LORD weighs hearts. Doing what is right and just pleases him more than sacrifice. The plans of the careful lead to plenty. Whoever ignores the cry of the poor will cry and not be heard. Justice brings joy to the righteous. The sacrifice of the wicked is hateful. The horse is made ready for battle, and victory belongs to the LORD.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the chapter place fair conduct above an offering?

contextNote.title: Ritual cannot substitute for justice
contextNote.text: Verse 3 ranks right conduct above offerings. The prophets say the same in 1 Samuel 15:22 and Hosea 6:6. Micah 6:6–8 asks the question at length. The wisdom teachers and the prophets agree here. Verse 27 goes further about worship offered with evil intent. Verse 13 gives one concrete test. A person who ignores the poor will find his own cry ignored.

passages.title: A good name and fair treatment
passages.summary: A good name is better than great riches. The rich and the poor have this in common: the LORD made them both. Train a child in the way he should go. The borrower is servant to the lender. A generous person is blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor. Then a new set of sayings begins. Do not rob the poor or crush the needy in court. The LORD will take up their case.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Scripture Helps teaches loving correction and rejects using the rod to justify abuse. Why does the teacher mention God when forbidding harm to poor people?

contextNote.title: A shared maker limits social divisions
contextNote.text: Verse 2 does not deny the gap between rich and poor. Verse 7 admits that the rich rule and lenders hold power. Verse 2 says where the two “meet.” One Maker formed them both. Neither stands higher before him. Verses 22–23 draw out a result for the courts. The LORD himself argues the case of the poor.

passages.title: Control appetite and protect others’ property
passages.summary: At a ruler’s table, the learner must control his appetite. He should not wear himself out to get rich, for wealth flies away. He should not eat with a stingy host. He must not move old boundary stones or take orphans’ fields. Their Redeemer is strong. He should listen to his father and not despise his mother when she is old. The chapter ends with a picture of a drunk person. He is beaten, feels nothing, and wants another drink.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the teacher warn against entering the fields of fatherless children?

contextNote.title: Hospitality may carry a hidden price
contextNote.text: Verses 6–8 describe a host who resents what his guest eats. He says, “Eat and drink,” and his heart is not in it (verse 7). He counts each bite. The meal becomes a debt the guest did not agree to. Verses 1–3 gave a similar warning about a ruler’s table. Both passages treat a dinner as a place of hidden bargaining. Verses 10–11 name God as the defender of orphans’ land.

passages.title: Rescue people and examine your work
passages.summary: Do not envy evil people or wish to be with them. A house is built by wisdom. If you give up in a hard time, your strength is small. Rescue those being led away to death. You cannot say you did not know, for God weighs hearts. A righteous person falls seven times and rises again. Do not rejoice when your enemy falls. The teacher passes a lazy man’s field and learns from its thorns.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What excuse does the teacher reject when someone needs rescue?

contextNote.title: Knowing creates a duty to act
contextNote.text: Verse 11 gives a duty: rescue people being taken to their death. Verse 12 closes the usual excuse. Someone may say, “We didn’t know this.” God weighs hearts and knows whether that is true. He can tell real ignorance from a choice not to look. Knowing creates a duty to act. Verses 30–34 show the teacher learning by looking at a ruined field.

passages.title: Hezekiah’s men collect Solomon’s sayings
passages.summary: These are more sayings of Solomon, copied by the men of King Hezekiah. God’s glory is to hide a matter, and a king’s is to search it out. Do not push yourself forward before a king. Do not rush to court against a neighbor. A fitting word is like gold apples in a silver setting. A soft tongue can break a bone. If your enemy is hungry, give him food. A person without self-control is like a city with broken walls.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What does feeding a hungry enemy require beyond winning an argument?

contextNote.title: Collected sayings connect wisdom with government
contextNote.text: Verse 1 says Hezekiah’s men copied this collection. That was long after Solomon’s time (2 Kings 18:1). Royal scribes cared for these sayings. Verse 2 then describes a king’s proper work. God’s world holds more than its surface shows. A ruler honors his office by finding out the truth of a matter. Verse 8 applies that: do not hurry into court.

passages.title: Choose when to answer foolish speech
passages.summary: Honor does not suit a fool, like snow in summer. An undeserved curse does not land. Do not answer a fool by his folly, or you will be like him. Answer a fool by his folly, or he will think himself wise. A proverb in a fool’s mouth is useless. The lazy person says a lion is in the road. A meddler in another’s quarrel grabs a dog by the ears. Without wood a fire goes out, and without gossip a quarrel ends.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How can the two warnings in verses 4–5 fit different situations?

contextNote.title: Paired sayings require judgment
contextNote.text: Verses 4 and 5 contradict each other on purpose. One says not to answer a fool, and the next says to answer him. Each gives a good reason. Silence avoids sinking to his level. A reply keeps him from thinking he has won. The reader must judge which fits the moment. Verses 7 and 9 warn that a proverb in the wrong mouth does harm.

passages.title: Care for friends and flocks
passages.summary: Do not boast about tomorrow. Let another person praise you, not your own mouth. Wounds from a friend can be trusted. A neighbor nearby is better than a brother far away. As iron sharpens iron, one person sharpens another. A person is tested by the praise he receives. Know the state of your flocks, for riches do not last. The lambs will clothe you, and the goats will feed your household.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the teacher connect daily care for animals with the household’s future?

contextNote.title: Care requires knowledge of actual conditions
contextNote.text: The chapter ends with a short poem about herding (verses 23–27). Verse 23 says to “know well” the condition of the animals. A herder must look at the actual flock and not assume. Verse 24 gives the reason: wealth and even a crown do not last. A living flock renews itself if someone cares for it. Verse 27 includes the servant girls in what it provides. The friendship sayings in verses 6, 9, and 17 also ask for close attention.

passages.title: Honest poverty and harmful wealth
passages.summary: The wicked run when no one chases them, and the righteous are bold. A poor man who oppresses the poor is like rain that ruins the crop. It is better to be poor and honest than rich and crooked. Wealth built on high interest ends up with someone kind to the poor. Whoever hides his sins does not prosper. Whoever confesses and leaves them finds mercy. One who hurries to get rich will not go unpunished. Whoever gives to the poor will lack nothing.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Which actions show that a wealthy person has harmed poorer neighbors?

contextNote.title: Profit can reveal a damaged relationship
contextNote.text: Exodus 22:25 and Leviticus 25:36 forbid taking interest from a poor neighbor. Verse 8 describes someone who grows rich that way. The saying claims the money will not stay with him. It ends in the hands of a person who pities the poor. Proverbs states such things as the way God’s world tends to go. They are not promises for every single case. Verse 11 adds that a poor person with insight sees through the rich.

passages.title: Rulers, anger, and teaching children
passages.summary: A person who is often corrected and stays stubborn will suddenly break. When the righteous increase, the people rejoice. A king builds up the land by justice. The righteous care about justice for the poor. A fool lets out all his anger. The poor and the oppressor both receive sight from the LORD. Where there is no vision, the people cast off restraint. Fear of people is a trap, and trust in the LORD keeps one safe.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does hearing a poor person’s case affect a ruler’s work?

contextNote.title: Justice requires learning the poor person’s case
contextNote.text: Verse 7 says the righteous “care about” the rights of the poor. Caring here includes learning the facts of their case. That takes time and effort. The wicked, the verse says, have no interest in such knowledge. Not caring becomes a kind of ignorance. Verse 14 applies the point to kings who judge. Verse 13 repeats that the LORD gives light to both poor and powerful.

passages.title: Agur asks for enough
passages.summary: These are the words of Agur. He says he is too ignorant to know the Holy One. Every word of God is tested and true. He asks God for two things before he dies. He wants lies kept far away. He wants neither poverty nor riches, only the food he needs. If full, he might deny the LORD, and if poor, he might steal. The chapter then gives lists of things that come in threes and fours.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does Agur ask for neither poverty nor riches?

contextNote.title: A prayer questions both extremes of wealth
contextNote.text: Verses 7–9 are the only prayer in the book of Proverbs. Agur sees danger at both ends of wealth. Verse 9 explains each one. A full person may ask, “Who is the LORD?” A hungry person may steal and dishonor God’s name. So verse 8 asks for the food that is needed. Jesus teaches a similar request for daily bread in Matthew 6:11.

passages.title: A mother advises a king
passages.summary: These are the words King Lemuel’s mother taught him. A king must not waste his strength or dull his mind with wine. Otherwise he will forget the law and wrong the afflicted. He must speak for those who cannot speak. He must judge fairly and defend the poor and needy. A poem then praises a capable wife. She buys a field, trades, clothes her household, and gives to the poor. Charm and beauty pass, and a woman who fears the LORD is praised.
passages.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me praises the woman’s strength, skill, and influence. How do the woman’s business decisions help both her household and poor neighbors?

contextNote.title: A mother’s instruction reaches public judgment
contextNote.text: The king’s teacher here is his mother, as in 1:8. Verse 8 gives her view of what power is for. A king should open his mouth for the “mute.” These are people who have no voice in court. Verse 9 adds fair judgment for the poor and needy. The poem in verses 10–31 then shows wisdom at work in a household. The book began with Wisdom as a woman and ends with a wise woman.

events.title: Listen before joining others
events.summary: The book opens by stating its purpose: to teach wisdom, justice, and good sense. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. A parent tells a son to listen to his father and mother. Sinners will invite him to ambush the innocent and share the loot. He must not go with them. They set a trap for their own lives. Then Wisdom calls aloud in the street like a woman. Those who refuse her will eat the fruit of their own choices.
events.detail: Verse 8 names two teachers, a father and a mother. The mother’s teaching stands beside the father’s instruction. Verse 9 calls their words a wreath and a necklace. The first lesson that follows is about an invitation (verses 10–14). A gang says, “Come with us,” and promises one shared purse. The learner must choose between two sets of voices. Verses 18–19 say the violent men ambush themselves.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me explains fearing God as love and obedience. Why does Wisdom warn that the violent men trap themselves?

events.title: Search for wisdom
events.summary: The teacher tells his son to accept his words and store up his commands. He must turn his ear to wisdom and call out for understanding. He must seek it like silver and search for it like hidden treasure. Then he will understand the fear of the LORD. The LORD gives wisdom and guards the path of the just. Good sense will protect the learner from men who speak twisted things. It will protect him from the unfaithful wife. The upright will remain in the land.
events.detail: Verses 1–4 stack up conditions with the word “if.” Verse 5 answers with “then.” Verse 4 compares the search to mining for silver. Miners dig long and deep for what they value. Yet verse 6 says the LORD gives wisdom. The chapter holds both together. A person must search hard, and what he finds is still a gift.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me invites readers to seek wisdom from God. Which actions does the teacher compare with searching for treasure?

events.title: Trust God and help neighbors
events.summary: The teacher tells his son to keep kindness and truth close. He should trust the LORD with all his heart, not his own insight. He should honor the LORD with his wealth. The LORD corrects those he loves, as a father does. Wisdom is worth more than silver and is a tree of life. The learner must not hold back good from one who is owed it. He must not tell a neighbor to come back tomorrow. He must not plot against a neighbor who lives trustingly beside him.
events.detail: The chapter begins with trust in God (verses 5–6). It ends with neighbors (verses 27–30). Verse 27 speaks of good that is “due” to someone. The neighbor has a claim, and the learner has the means. Verse 28 names a common way to refuse: come again tomorrow. Delay can be a quiet form of saying no. Trust in God shows itself in prompt help.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me teaches trust in the Lord. Why should the learner help a neighbor today rather than tomorrow?

events.title: Choose a path carefully
events.summary: A father tells his sons to listen and gain understanding. He says he was once a tender son himself. His own father taught him to get wisdom above all else. He warns against the path of the wicked. The path of the righteous is like dawn that grows to full day. The learner must guard his heart, for life flows from it. He must keep his mouth honest and his eyes straight ahead. He must make his path level and not turn aside.
events.detail: In verse 3 the teacher remembers being a child. His father taught him the words he now repeats (verse 4). Three generations stand in these verses. The teaching is handed on; the father did not invent it. Verse 23 puts the heart first as the source of life. Verses 24–27 then name the mouth, the eyes, and the feet. Guarding the inside comes before guarding the steps.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects the path image with following the Lord. How do speech, sight, and steps affect the path the learner follows?

events.title: Remain faithful to your wife
events.summary: The teacher warns his son about another man’s wife. Her lips drip honey, but the end is bitter. Her steps lead down to death. He must stay far from her door. Otherwise strangers will take his strength and wealth, and he will groan at the end. He should drink water from his own well. He should rejoice in the wife of his youth. A man’s ways are before the LORD, and his own sins bind him.
events.detail: Verses 15–18 speak of faithfulness through pictures of water. A cistern, a well, springs, and a fountain are named. In a dry land a household’s water was precious and guarded. Verse 16 pictures it spilled in the streets and wasted. The chapter does more than forbid. Verses 18–19 tell the man to delight in his own wife. The warning rests on a good thing worth keeping.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What costs does the teacher describe beyond the first attraction?

events.title: Promises, work, and harmful acts
events.summary: The teacher warns against pledging to cover another person’s debt. If the son has done so, he must free himself at once. He tells the lazy person to watch the ant. She has no ruler and still stores food in summer. A little extra sleep brings poverty like a robber. A troublemaker winks and stirs up quarrels. The LORD hates seven things, including lying and shedding innocent blood. Adultery is like carrying fire in one’s lap.
events.detail: Verse 6 sends the learner to watch an insect. Wisdom can be gained by looking closely at the created world. Verse 7 notes that the ant has no chief or overseer. She works without being told. Verse 8 adds that she works at the right season. The chapter covers debts, laziness, troublemakers, and adultery. In each case a small lapse of attention leads to a large loss.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does the ant’s work differ from the sleeper’s choices?

events.title: A learner follows a tempting invitation
events.summary: The teacher tells his son to treat wisdom as a sister. Then he describes what he saw from his window. A young man without sense walked near a certain woman’s corner at dusk. She came out dressed to attract him and seized and kissed him. She said she had made offerings and prepared her bed with fine linen. Her husband was away on a long journey. He followed her like an ox going to slaughter. Her house is the road to the grave.
events.detail: The warning comes as a scene the teacher watched (verses 6–7). The details matter. Verse 8 says the youth walked toward her corner, so he chose the street. Verse 9 marks the time as twilight turning to dark. Her speech uses religion (verse 14) and promises no one will know (verses 19–20). Verses 22–23 compare him to an ox, a deer, and a bird. A story lets the learner see the steps before the fall.
events.uncertainty: Egypt names the cloth’s origin, not the scene’s location.

lds.text: Which details show the difference between her promises and the danger?

events.title: Wisdom speaks in public
events.summary: Wisdom calls out on the heights and at the city gates. She speaks to all people and says her words are true. She is better than silver, gold, and rubies. By her kings rule justly. She loves those who love her. The LORD had her at the beginning, before the mountains and the seas. She was beside him when he marked out the earth’s foundations. Whoever finds her finds life.
events.detail: Wisdom speaks in the open, at the gates where everyone passes (verse 3). The woman of chapter 7 worked at dusk in a side street. In verse 22 Wisdom gives her age. She was with the LORD before any of his works. Verses 27–30 place her beside him at creation. So living wisely fits the way the world was made. Verses 30–31 add that she rejoiced in the world and in people.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me points to the rejection of evil in verse 13. How does Wisdom’s public invitation differ from the woman’s invitation in chapter 7?

events.title: Two women invite the learner
events.summary: Wisdom has built her house with seven pillars. She has prepared meat and wine and set her table. She sends her maids to call from the high places. She invites the simple to come in and eat. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. Folly is a loud woman who sits at her door. She calls to the simple with the same words. She offers stolen water, and her guests are in the grave.
events.detail: Verse 4 and verse 16 are the same invitation, word for word. Two hosts call the same people in the same way. The learner must look past the words to what each has ready. Wisdom built a house and cooked a meal (verses 1–2). Folly offers stolen water and secret bread (verse 17). Verse 6 ends in life, and verse 18 ends among the dead. This chapter closes the book’s long opening lessons.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What does Folly hide that Wisdom openly explains?

events.title: Words and work affect others
events.summary: Here the short sayings of Solomon begin. A wise son makes his father glad. Wealth gained by wrong does no good. Lazy hands make a person poor, and hard work brings wealth. Love covers all wrongs. Where words are many, sin is not far away. The lips of the righteous feed many people. When the storm passes, the wicked are gone, and the righteous stand.
events.detail: From this chapter the sayings stand alone, two lines each. The second line often contrasts with the first. No story surrounds them. The reader must supply the situation where each one fits. Verse 19 says more talk gives more room for wrong. Restraint of the lips is called wisdom. Many sayings in this chapter concern speech (verses 11, 13, 18, 20–21, 31–32).
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does hatred stir up quarrels while love covers offenses?

events.title: Honesty in trade and community
events.summary: A false scale is hateful to the LORD, and honest weights please him. Pride brings shame, and humility brings wisdom. A city rejoices when the righteous do well. A gossip reveals secrets, and a trustworthy person keeps them. Many advisers bring safety. One person gives freely and gains more. Another holds back and becomes poor. People curse the one who hoards grain.
events.detail: Verse 1 calls a rigged scale an “abomination.” Other texts use that strong word for idols. Leviticus 19:35–36 and Deuteronomy 25:13–16 give the law behind it. A buyer could not easily test a seller’s weights. The poor, who bought in small amounts, were hurt most. An ancient trade weight shows the kind of tool the saying has in view. Verse 26 applies the same concern to those who hoard grain.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does withholding grain affect the people who need it?

events.title: Correction, work, and careful speech
events.summary: Whoever loves correction loves knowledge. A worthy wife is her husband’s crown. A righteous person cares for the life of his animal. The one who works his land has bread. A fool thinks his own way is right. Rash words cut like a sword, and a wise tongue heals. Truthful lips last forever. Worry weighs a heart down, and a kind word makes it glad.
events.detail: Verse 18 treats words as a weapon or a medicine. The harmful speaker is called rash. He may not mean harm; he simply does not think first. The wound is as real as a sword cut. The wise tongue is said to heal. Verse 25 gives an example: one good word lifts a heavy heart. Verse 19 adds that true words last and lies do not.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the chapter compare rash speech with a sword?

events.title: Choose teachers and companions
events.summary: A wise son accepts his father’s teaching. The one who guards his mouth guards his life. Some pretend to be rich and have nothing. Wealth gained in haste shrinks away. Hope put off makes the heart sick. Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise. A poor person’s field may yield much food, and injustice sweeps it away. A parent who loves a child corrects him.
events.detail: Verse 12 gives no command. It describes what waiting does to a person. A hope delayed again and again makes the heart sick. A longing fulfilled is called a tree of life. Verse 19 repeats that a desire met is sweet. The saying helps a reader understand another person’s weariness. Verse 23 adds that poverty can come from injustice, not from laziness.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Scripture Helps applies the rod image to loving, consistent teaching. How does verse 23 challenge blaming every poor person for poverty?

events.title: Look beyond first impressions
events.summary: A wise woman builds her house, and a foolish one tears it down. A way may seem right to a person and end in death. Even in laughter the heart may ache. The simple believe everything, and the careful watch their steps. The poor are shunned even by neighbors, and the rich have many friends. Whoever oppresses the poor insults their Maker. A calm heart gives life to the body. Righteousness lifts up a nation.
events.detail: This chapter keeps setting how things seem against how they are. Verse 12 says a road can look right and lead to death. Verse 13 applies that to a face. A person may laugh while the heart is in pain. Verse 10 says each heart knows its own bitterness. So the reader should be slow to judge by appearances. Verse 31 ties the treatment of the poor to respect for God.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why should the learner look beyond laughter when judging someone’s happiness?

events.title: Answer gently and accept advice
events.summary: A gentle answer turns away anger, and a harsh word stirs it up. The eyes of the LORD are in every place. A little with the fear of the LORD is better than great treasure with trouble. A meal of vegetables with love is better than rich meat with hatred. Plans fail without advice. A word spoken at the right time is good. The LORD hears the prayer of the righteous. Humility comes before honor.
events.detail: Verse 1 says the direction of a quarrel depends on the reply. A gentle answer is not a weak one. It “turns away” wrath, which is an active result. A harsh word feeds the fire. Verse 18 says a patient person calms a dispute. Verse 28 says the righteous think before they answer. Verse 23 praises the word that comes at the right moment.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me teaches kind words and patient answers. How do gentle words change the direction of a quarrel?

events.title: Plans need humility and self-control
events.summary: People make plans in their hearts, and the answer comes from the LORD. A person’s ways seem pure to him, and the LORD weighs motives. Honest scales belong to the LORD. Pride goes before destruction. Pleasant words are like honey. Gray hair is a crown of glory. One who controls his temper is better than one who captures a city. The lot is cast, and its every decision is from the LORD.
events.detail: Verse 9 keeps two truths together. People plan their course, and the saying does not discourage that. The LORD directs the actual steps. Verses 1 and 33 make the same point at the chapter’s two ends. Outcomes are not fully in human hands. That leads to the warning about pride in verse 18. Verse 32 values rule over oneself above victory in war.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me applies these sayings to how people communicate. Why does the chapter value controlling anger above capturing a city?

events.title: Peace, friendship, and fair judgment
events.summary: A dry crust with peace is better than a house full of feasting with strife. The LORD tests hearts as fire tests silver and gold. Whoever mocks the poor insults their Maker. One who covers an offense seeks love. A friend loves at all times. To clear the guilty and condemn the innocent are both hateful to the LORD. A cheerful heart is good medicine. Even a fool seems wise when he keeps silent.
events.detail: Verse 1 is a “better than” saying. It compares a dry scrap with a table full of meat. The peace at the table decides which is better. A feast with quarreling is the poorer meal. Sayings in 15:16–17 make the same judgment. Verse 14 adds advice on how to keep that peace. A quarrel starts like a leak in a dam, so stop it early.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How do repeated accusations damage a friendship?

events.title: Listen before answering
events.summary: A person who keeps apart seeks only his own desire. A fool takes no pleasure in understanding and only airs his opinions. The name of the LORD is a strong tower. A rich man imagines his wealth is a high wall. To answer before listening is folly and shame. The first to state a case seems right until the other side questions him. Death and life are in the power of the tongue. Some friends stay closer than a brother.
events.detail: Verse 13 states a basic rule of fairness and of courtesy. A person must hear before he answers. Verse 17 applies the rule to disputes. The first speaker sounds right until the other side is heard. Verse 2 describes the opposite habit. The fool wants to talk and not to understand. Verse 15 says the ear of the wise seeks knowledge.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why should a judge hear more than the first person’s account?

events.title: Wealth changes how people treat neighbors
events.summary: It is better to be poor and honest than a liar and a fool. Zeal without knowledge is not good. Wealth brings many friends, and a poor person loses the one he has. A false witness will not go unpunished. Good sense makes a person slow to anger. Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD. People make many plans, and the LORD’s purpose stands. A lazy person will not even lift his hand to his mouth.
events.detail: Verse 4 reports a fact about money and friendship. It does not approve of it. Verses 6–7 add that even a poor man’s brothers avoid him. The chapter then judges what it has observed. Verse 17 says kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD. Verses 1 and 22 say an honest poor person is better than a liar. The saying trains the reader to notice how wealth bends loyalty.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: How does the chapter expose friendships that depend on wealth?

events.title: Trade honestly and avoid revenge
events.summary: Wine is a mocker, and whoever is led astray by it is not wise. It is an honor to stay out of a quarrel. A person’s purpose is like deep water, and a wise one draws it out. No one can say his heart is fully clean. The LORD hates unequal weights and measures. A buyer says “It’s no good” and then boasts of his bargain. Do not say you will repay evil. Wait for the LORD.
events.detail: Verse 10 speaks of “differing weights.” A cheating trader kept two sets, one heavy and one light. He bought with one and sold with the other. Deuteronomy 25:13–14 forbids keeping both in the bag. Verse 23 repeats the saying in this same chapter. Verse 14 shows the buyer lying too. An ancient trade weight shows the kind of tool the saying has in view.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What does the buyer’s changed story reveal about his honesty?

events.title: Justice matters more than offerings
events.summary: A king’s heart is in the LORD’s hand like a stream of water. The LORD weighs hearts. Doing what is right and just pleases him more than sacrifice. The plans of the careful lead to plenty. Whoever ignores the cry of the poor will cry and not be heard. Justice brings joy to the righteous. The sacrifice of the wicked is hateful. The horse is made ready for battle, and victory belongs to the LORD.
events.detail: Verse 3 ranks right conduct above offerings. The prophets say the same in 1 Samuel 15:22 and Hosea 6:6. Micah 6:6–8 asks the question at length. The wisdom teachers and the prophets agree here. Verse 27 goes further about worship offered with evil intent. Verse 13 gives one concrete test. A person who ignores the poor will find his own cry ignored.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the chapter place fair conduct above an offering?

events.title: A good name and fair treatment
events.summary: A good name is better than great riches. The rich and the poor have this in common: the LORD made them both. Train a child in the way he should go. The borrower is servant to the lender. A generous person is blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor. Then a new set of sayings begins. Do not rob the poor or crush the needy in court. The LORD will take up their case.
events.detail: Verse 2 does not deny the gap between rich and poor. Verse 7 admits that the rich rule and lenders hold power. Verse 2 says where the two “meet.” One Maker formed them both. Neither stands higher before him. Verses 22–23 draw out a result for the courts. The LORD himself argues the case of the poor.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Scripture Helps teaches loving correction and rejects using the rod to justify abuse. Why does the teacher mention God when forbidding harm to poor people?

events.title: Control appetite and protect others’ property
events.summary: At a ruler’s table, the learner must control his appetite. He should not wear himself out to get rich, for wealth flies away. He should not eat with a stingy host. He must not move old boundary stones or take orphans’ fields. Their Redeemer is strong. He should listen to his father and not despise his mother when she is old. The chapter ends with a picture of a drunk person. He is beaten, feels nothing, and wants another drink.
events.detail: Verses 6–8 describe a host who resents what his guest eats. He says, “Eat and drink,” and his heart is not in it (verse 7). He counts each bite. The meal becomes a debt the guest did not agree to. Verses 1–3 gave a similar warning about a ruler’s table. Both passages treat a dinner as a place of hidden bargaining. Verses 10–11 name God as the defender of orphans’ land.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: Why does the teacher warn against entering the fields of fatherless children?

events.title: Rescue people and examine your work
events.summary: Do not envy evil people or wish to be with them. A house is built by wisdom. If you give up in a hard time, your strength is small. Rescue those being led away to death. You cannot say you did not know, for God weighs hearts. A righteous person falls seven times and rises again. Do not rejoice when your enemy falls. The teacher passes a lazy man’s field and learns from its thorns.
events.detail: Verse 11 gives a duty: rescue people being taken to their death. Verse 12 closes the usual excuse. Someone may say, “We didn’t know this.” God weighs hearts and knows whether that is true. He can tell real ignorance from a choice not to look. Knowing creates a duty to act. Verses 30–34 show the teacher learning by looking at a ruined field.
events.uncertainty: The chapter does not name a place for a map marker.

lds.text: What excuse does the teacher reject when someone needs rescue?

events.title: Hezekiah’s men collect Solomon’s sayings
events.summary: These are more sayings of Solomon, copied by the men of King Hezekiah. God’s glory is to hide a matter, and a king’s is to search it out. Do not push yourself forward before a king. Do not rush to court against a neighbor. A fitting word is like gold apples in a silver setting. A soft tongue can break a bone. If your enemy is hungry, give him food. steps.title: Wisdom begins with relationships
steps.text: Verse 8 names two teachers, a father and a mother. The mother’s teaching stands beside the father’s instruction. Verse 9 calls their words a wreath and a necklace. The first lesson that follows is about an invitation (verses 10–14). A gang says, “Come with us,” and promises one shared purse. The learner must choose between two sets of voices. Verses 18–19 say the violent men ambush themselves.

steps.title: A proverb makes trade a moral decision
steps.text: Verse 1 calls a rigged scale an “abomination.” Other texts use that strong word for idols. Leviticus 19:35–36 and Deuteronomy 25:13–16 give the law behind it. A buyer could not easily test a seller’s weights. The poor, who bought in small amounts, were hurt most. An ancient trade weight shows the kind of tool the saying has in view. Verse 26 applies the same concern to those who hoard grain.
